title: Meeting Johnny Dodds at the One Cent Club, Chicago
summary: Russell visits Johnny Dodds in 1936 at a Depression-era club, with a digression on New Orleans bands replaying numbers and the Saints.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: 1949. It says here she was approximately later, 11 years older than George Bakke. I figured that out. To get on to a few other people that I used to talk to, the next one on this list was Johnny Dodds, whose notes I'll have to send. They probably are in a box of Baby Dodds notes, I think. I was always going to try to rewrite them. When I first met Johnny Dodds about 1936, I went to Chicago and I inquired if he was playing anyplace or where he was. All I knew about him, he'd been on some of the jelly roll records and especially the Louis Hot Fives. Of course, his name is called off. You couldn't miss that on that Gut Bucket Blues when Louis introduces all the numbers. So everybody knew Johnny Dodds was on quite a few of those early records. So at that time, he was playing at a place called the One Cent Club. It was out at, I think, Roger Park Elevator Station, which I don't believe is running now, in the west part of Chicago, either north or south, I'm not sure. The what? Roger Park.

Yes. Right at the end of the line. You go to the end of the line and this place, the One Cent Club, it means that you buy one drink at the regular price and you get a second drink for one cent. It was during the Depression, of course. They had on big blue silk blouses with big long full sleeves, you know, sort of like clowns wear. Not that they were trying to make clowns out of them, but I mean, it was a special uniform they wore. A drummer, I believe it must have been, I'm not sure, unless I, until I look up my notes, if I did write it down, even I doubt that I did. Probably Tubby Hall and the pianist was another Alexander. I can't think of his first name, but it wasn't Charlie Alexander who had played with him on some of the early records. But as soon as I told him I had his old records and I said, I'm going to play a piece, see if you know what it is. Of all things, it was high society, which anybody ought to know, although in those days it wasn't the, the nuisance it is. Now they play it almost like they do the Saints Go Marching In. Bunk always got so sick of it in New York where everybody would request it. Oh, two or three times a night. Oh, here's a thing I might mention, which I wanted to try to get Johnny Wiggs talking more about the different styles that they played pieces in and the dances, the way they did things. A year or two ago, he was trying to tell me a lot of stuff about New Orleans Band, some real good stuff. Don't remember now exactly what it was about, but he said he'd tell me later. I'd always say, don't tell me now, you'll forget it when you get on tape and think you've told. Anyway, he couldn't think what it was. But here's one little point that's quite characteristic of New Orleans music. In the old days, I understand, they played almost everything twice. It would hardly ever be that they'd play a thing. If the dancers clapped at all, I used to question Bunk about this. Even, say, 15 years ago when I'd go to any dance that Bunk played down here or around here, the George Lewis or any of those bands would play, if the people clapped at all, they'd play it over again, sometimes almost as long, maybe even longer, but usually a little bit shorter. If they played maybe 10 choruses the first time, they might play five or six the next time. And they still do that, even over at Preservation Hall, I noticed I'm surprised. a couple of times this summer they'd get into that and people clapped, which they did maybe more enthusiastically than usual. They'd play those over again. So in New York when they'd have a certain thing like the Saints, that's where the Saints started getting popular. Louis had made the Saints, not really popular, but he'd made this record in 1937 or 1938 and it caught on in a way. It was in the jukeboxes, but still the other small jazz band, and the other so-called Dixieland band leaders didn't pick it up. Nobody else played it much. But Bunk had recorded it and then he played it in New York maybe six or seven times a night and all the other bands saw how popular it was and so they all started recording it and playing it.
